      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/28/egypt-lina-attalah-mada-masr-press-freedom-clampdown</link>
      <description><p>Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website</p><p>Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.</p><p>Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/28/egypt-lina-attalah-mada-masr-press-freedom-clampdown">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/28/africa-ebola-outbreak-could-reach-uk-says-top-health-official</link>
      <description><p>Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment</p><p>The “unprecedented” <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/aug/17/what-is-ebola-why-who-says-drc-uganda-outbreak-global-health-emergency">spread of the Ebola outbreak</a> means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.</p><p>As the current outbreak reached <a href="https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/ebola-disease-multi-country-outbreak-2026">10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths</a>, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/28/africa-ebola-outbreak-could-reach-uk-says-top-health-official">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/26/us-forces-accused-of-weaponising-somalia-flood-el-nino</link>
      <description><p><strong>Exclusive:</strong> Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy?</p><p>The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.</p><p>“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/26/us-forces-accused-of-weaponising-somalia-flood-el-nino">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Watered-down version of statement to be issued at end of Montreal summit instead offers ‘ever closer association’</p><p>The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between member states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.</p><p>A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/28/european-union-canada">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Treasury denies Healey plan to cut welfare bill before election, claiming his comments were misinterpreted – UK politics live</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/politics/live/2026/oct/29/budget-john-healey-labour-uk-politics-latest-news</link>
      <description><p>Asked earlier if there would be a cut to the welfare bill before the next election, the chancellor said: ‘There will be a reduction in the benefits bill’</p><p><strong>John Healey</strong> is rowing back from his answer in an interview in the Today programme implying he wanted welfare spending to go down before the next general election. According to <strong>Chris Mason</strong>, the BBC’s political editor, Treasury sources are saying his words have been over-interpreted.</p><p>This relates to what Healey said in an interview with Nick Robinson for the Today programme. It was broadcast this morning, but recorded yesterday, and the BBC has written it up in<a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5ynwkjgpz3o"> a story</a> on its website headlined: “Healey promises reduction in welfare bill before next election”.</p><p><strong>Robinson: </strong>Let’s take welfare if we could. £19bn up in the year ahead. That’s the entire police budget for England and Wales. That’s the entire annual defence equipment budget. And yet in your speech you said, well, we’ve got a couple of reports coming next month, then we’ll have a white paper, which in non-Westminster jargon means a consultation, then you’ll have some legislation, then you’ll have a row in the Labour party. You’re not going to make any of these cuts before the next election, are you?</p><p><strong>Healey:</strong> Well first, I’ve said clearly, the prime minister said as well, we have to bring the benefits bill down. You don’t do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures. We do have a big report, two big reports being produced next month, that will help us map out the way that we need to change the system for the long run. We are in fact reducing and have been over the last two years the rate of increase in the welfare bill compared to the previous period – I’m afraid to say – of a broken system the Conservatives put in place. We’re bringing back and have brought back face to face assessments which they axed for instance. We’ve been changing universal credits so people aren’t branding themselves as too sick to work in order to make that system work better.</p><p><em>There will be. [Direct answer to Robinson’s question.] There will be a reduction in the benefits bill [etc etc – Healey expanding on the answer.]</em></p><p><em>There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill</em> [Healey simply repeating three words as he launches into more general answer, not answering Robinson directly, but just explaining the government’s approach.]</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/live/2026/oct/29/budget-john-healey-labour-uk-politics-latest-news">Continue reading...</a></description>
